title: Hedy Lamarr's Life In Reverse | From a Florida Home to a Vienna Apartment
description:
Hedy Lamarr's life runs backwards in this episode, opening at her death in Florida in January 2000 and rewinding to her birth in Vienna in November 1914. The journey steps through the patents she shared with a composer in 1940 and 1941, the studio contract that renamed her in 1937, the arms dealer she fled in 1937, and the school in the Döbling district where she grew up. Every scene moves to an earlier year, so the wireless invention appears before the film career that hid it. Dates, patent numbers and contracts follow the documented record, and reports about her later years are stated plainly.

scenes.narration: In 2014 the National Inventors Hall of Fame inducted her and the composer she worked with, for a patent on hopping between radio frequencies. That method sits under Bluetooth, wireless networks and the signals that phones use every day. The recognition came a century after her birth and fourteen years after her death.

On January 19, 2000, Hedy Lamarr died at her home in Florida at the age of eighty five. She had been away from the screen for four decades, and the film studios had long since stopped calling. The patent that outlived her work was still on the record in Washington, where she had never collected a fee from it.

Three years earlier, in 1997, she and the composer George Antheil had been given a pioneer award by an American electronic rights group, which honoured them for the frequency hopping system. He had been dead for some years, and she was sent the award. Reporters called, and she told them that she had expected the recognition much earlier.

Ten years before that, in 1990, a business magazine had tracked her down and printed an interview in which she said she could not understand why nobody acknowledged her work, since it was being used all over the world. The interview brought a fresh wave of attention, and it was the first serious discussion of her engineering in the American press.

Through the 1970s and 1980s she had lived quietly, away from the film industry, in flats where the curtains stayed closed and the telephone rang little. She had been married six times and had three children, and the money from her films did not last. The patent office held her one important document, and nobody in her building knew it.

Thirty five years earlier, in 1965, her sixth marriage had ended in divorce. She had married in 1933, 1939, 1943, 1951, 1953 and 1963, and every one of them was over within a few years. She kept her own name, which had been given to her by a studio chief, and she kept working as long as parts were offered.

Five years before that, in 1960, the city of Los Angeles gave her a star on the pavement of Hollywood Boulevard. The film work was behind her by then and the parts had grown smaller, but the studio still counted her among the names that had drawn audiences through the 1940s.

Two years earlier, in 1958, her last film had been released and she retired from acting at the age of forty three. She had made around thirty pictures over twenty five years, moving from one studio contract to the next. After that she gave occasional interviews and little else.

Five years before that, in April 1953, she had become a citizen of the United States, taking an oath in a court room after sixteen years in the country. She had arrived with a film contract in 1937 and had been stateless for the years in between, since her Austrian citizenship ended with her marriage.

Four years earlier, in 1949, she had played the title role in a biblical epic for a famous director, which became the biggest earner of her career. The picture filled cinemas and her face was on posters across the country. She was thirty four, and the studio placed her among its leading women for the rest of the decade.

Six years earlier, in 1943, she had married a British actor, and their daughter was born in 1945 and their son in 1947. She kept acting through those years and hired help for the children. The family life was short, and the marriage itself was over by 1947, with the divorce following a few years later.

In August 1942 the patent office in Washington issued number 2292387 for a secret communication system in the name of Hedy Kiesler Markey, her legal name at the time. She and Antheil had given the rights to the American navy. The navy tested it and said the mechanism was too large for a torpedo, and the idea was set aside.

A year earlier, in 1941, the application had been drafted with the help of a patent firm and an engineering professor in California, who checked the electrical details. She understood the problem from her years at her first husband's table, where buyers of arms explained how radio controlled weapons could be jammed by an enemy transmitter.

In December 1940 the two of them had sent their idea to a government council set up to collect inventions for the war, and the council passed it on to engineers for comment. The proposal described a system that kept transmitter and receiver changing frequency together, so that an enemy jammer following one channel would lose the signal as both ends moved on.

By the autumn of 1940 they had the mechanism worked out. Antheil had written music for player pianos, and they used a clockwork drive with punched paper rolls to move both ends of a radio link through the same sequence at the same moment. The rolls came from the instruments he knew, and the electronics followed them.

Late in 1940 she had also been on a film set for one of the biggest pictures of the year, a story of oil fields and rival drillers that drew large audiences. She worked on the film during the day and met Antheil in the evenings, which left her little time for anything else in that season.

Earlier in 1940 she had met the composer at a dinner party in Hollywood. He was known for music written for machines with rolls, and she asked him about synchronized instruments. The conversation turned to torpedoes and radio interference, and the two of them began meeting to sketch a design.

In 1939 she was cast in parts that repeated her accent and her looks, playing nobles, wives of diplomats and women from other countries. The parts paid well and she took them. By then she was one of the better known actresses in the country, and the studio kept her busy.

In 1938 she had become famous in a single picture, a drama set in the narrow streets of a North African quarter opposite a leading French actor. The film did well in cinemas across America, and the studio announced her as a new star. She was twenty three, and the name she was given belonged to someone else.

The year before that, in 1937 and early 1938, a Hollywood boss had met her in London, offered her a contract, and renamed her after an actress he had admired in the silent era. He had her taught English, changed her hairstyle, and put her on a ship for California with five hundred dollars a week.

In 1937 she had left Europe for good, travelling first to Paris and then to London after her marriage became impossible to bear. Her husband was an Austrian maker of arms who kept her beside him at meetings with customers, and she had listened to all of it. She took a few pieces of jewellery and a train ticket west.

Between 1933 and 1937 she had been married to that arms manufacturer, whom she had met after her appearance in a Czech film. He was rich, older and controlling, and he bought up copies of the picture he disliked and kept her away from the screen. She attended dinners where weapons were sold, and learned what she needed later.

In 1933, at the age of eighteen, she had appeared in a Czech film with a love scene that made her notorious across Europe. The film was banned in several countries, including the United States, and her husband made efforts to destroy every copy. It was the part that made her famous, and the one she was never allowed to escape.

Two years earlier, in 1931, she had worked in the theatre under a famous Viennese and Berlin director, in a small role in a comedy. She was still a teenager and had left school for the stage. The work taught her how to hold a room, and it led straight to the film parts that followed.

In 1930, at fifteen or sixteen, she had been given a small part in a German film, her first. The picture gave her a line of dialogue and a place on a studio list, and it was enough to bring her to the attention of casting directors in Vienna and Berlin.

In the 1920s she had gone to a girls' school in the Döbling district of Vienna, on the northern edge of the city. At home her mother, a pianist, had her at the piano and in ballet classes. Her father, a bank director, took her on walks and talked her through printing presses, streetcars and other machines.

At the age of five, in 1919, she had taken apart a music box to find out how it made sound, and then put it together again. She later said that the moment taught her that anything could be taken apart and understood. Her father approved of the habit, and the house filled with small projects.

In those early years, before she was old enough for school, she walked in the woods outside Vienna with her father, who explained the workings of whatever they passed. She asked questions about the machines and got answers rather than silence, which was unusual for a girl of that time and place.

She was born Hedwig Eva Maria Kiesler on November 9, 1914, in Vienna, the only child of a bank director and his wife, in the middle of the first world war. Her family was of Jewish ancestry in a city where that would soon matter a great deal. She was called Hedy, and she grew up in comfort in the capital of the Austrian empire.
